title: The terminal: paths, files and permissions
summary_md: Session 9 opens Module 3 and turns the terminal you have used since session 3 into something you can reason about. It separates the terminal (the window), the shell (`bash` or `zsh`, which reads your line) and the operating system (which creates files and starts programs), and explains why a 50-year-old interface survived: it composes, it scripts, it works over `ssh`, and CI is a terminal. It then teaches the one tree under `/`, absolute and relative paths, and the rule that most "file not found" errors are the wrong current directory. It ends with managing files (`rm` is permanent) and permissions: no `x`, no run, and `chmod +x` is a statement that a file is a program.
exam_focus_md:
- A transcript with `pwd`, `cd` and an error such as `could not read expenses.csv`: say where the student is and what to type next (`pwd` first).
- A sequence of `cd` commands with `..`, `../..`, `~`, `cd -` or a plain `cd`: predict what `pwd` prints, or decide which of two paths names the same file.
- An `ls -l` or `ls -la` listing: which entries are folders, which are hidden, who can write, what can be run.
- The "permission denied" transcript: what is missing, what `chmod +x` states, why `./`, and why `chmod 777` is the wrong fix.
- Letters and numbers inside a judgement: 755 for `check.sh`, 600 for a private key, 644 for a normal file.
- Predicting what a careless `rm -r name *` removes, and naming the habits that prevent it.
- Linking the terminal to CI: the workflow is commands another computer types, `check.sh` needs its `x` bit committed (a diff with only `old mode 100644` / `new mode 100755`), and `/mnt/c` hides the problem.
- Not examined: flags as recall (`man`, `--help`, `whoami`, `df -h`, `top`, `nano`).

sections.heading: Terminal, shell and operating system
sections.body_md:
Session 9 starts by separating three things that people lump together as "the terminal".

| | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Terminal | The window. It shows text and sends your keystrokes | Windows Terminal, GNOME Terminal |
| Shell | The program inside it that reads a line and runs it | `bash`, `zsh` |
| Operating system | What actually creates files and starts programs | the Linux kernel |

When you type `touch notes/todo.txt` and press Enter, the terminal sends the characters, the shell reads the line, cuts it into words at the spaces and asks the operating system to start the program `touch`, and `touch` in turn asks the operating system to create the file.

**Terminal and shell swap independently. Your scripts depend on the shell.** You can change the window and keep `bash`, and nothing about your scripts changes. Change the shell and things can. That is why lab 00 cares which shell you run: WSL's Ubuntu gives you `bash`, every recent macOS gives you `zsh`, and the `uv` installer edits the startup file of your shell (`~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`). Even error messages belong to the shell: for the same problem, `bash` prints `bash: ./run.sh: Permission denied` and `zsh` prints `zsh: permission denied: ./run.sh`.

**Why a 50-year-old interface survived.** The slide gives four reasons:

- It composes. Small programs, joined by pipes (session 10).
- It scripts. Whatever you typed once, you can save and run again.
- It works over `ssh`. Every server you will ever touch has one, and nothing else.
- CI is a terminal. The check workflow is a list of commands someone else's computer types for you: `uv sync --locked`, `uv run ruff check .`, `uv run ruff format --check .`, `uv run mypy src tests`, `uv run pytest`.

The slide's summary is the line to remember: a GUI is for doing something once; a terminal is for doing it a hundred times. Running the checks before every push is the hundred-times case, and it is why Friday's `scripts/check.sh` exists. The slide closes with a note on the present: the current trend in AI-assisted development drops IDEs (integrated development environments) in favour of terminals.

One word, two ideas. In session 7, the imperative shell was the outer layer of your code (`cli.py`, which reads files, prints and exits). In session 9, the shell is the program that reads your command line. Keep them apart in an answer.
key_points: Terminal = the window; shell = the program that reads your line and runs it (`bash`, `zsh`); operating system = what creates files and starts programs.
Terminal and shell swap independently. Your scripts depend on the shell.
A GUI is for doing something once. A terminal is for doing it a hundred times.
CI is a terminal: the check workflow is a list of commands someone else's computer types for you.

sections.heading: One tree under /: where am I, what is here
sections.body_md:
Linux has one tree of folders with one root, written `/`. Everything is under `/`. There are no drive letters. Your home folder is `/home/alice` (on macOS, `/Users/alice`), and `~` is short for it, as is `$HOME`. The course keeps every project in `~/code`:

```text
/
├── home/
│   └── alice/              ← your home, ~
│       └── code/
│           └── my-project/
│               ├── .git/
│               ├── src/
│               └── pyproject.toml
├── etc/
└── usr/
```

On WSL, your Windows disk is part of the same tree, at `/mnt/c`. A project under `/mnt/c/Users/...` lives on the Windows filesystem: lab 00 warns that every `git` and `uv` operation there is several times slower, and section 8 shows that permissions do not work there either. Keep projects in your Linux home; `pwd` should start with `/home/`, not `/mnt/`.

Two commands answer the questions you ask most, "where am I?" and "what is here?" (slide 9):

```console
$ pwd
/home/alice/code/expense-tracker
$ ls
LICENSE  README.md  expenses.csv  pyproject.toml  src  tests  uv.lock
$ ls -a
.  ..  .git  .github  .gitignore  .python-version  LICENSE  README.md  ...
```

`ls` hides names that start with a dot. `.git` is one: that is why you never see it, and why it is safe. `ls -a` shows everything, and answers lab 09's first question: the entries that appear only with `-a` all start with a dot. Two of them are in every folder: `.` is the folder you are in, and `..` is its parent. The CI workflow is hidden the same way: in your group repository, `ls -la .github/workflows` shows `check.yml`.

The tree is also what `find` searches (lab 09, exercise 4). `find src tests -name "*.py"` lists the expense-tracker's six Python files at v0.4, three in each folder. `find` does not skip dot folders: run from the project root, `find . -name "test_*" -type f` also walks into `.venv`, where uv installed packages that ship their own test files, and, in a fresh clone right after `uv sync`, prints 44 paths instead of 3 (more once pytest has left `__pycache__` files in `tests`). Names repeat across the tree (`find ~/code -name tests -type d` finds one `tests` per project); the full path is what tells two files apart.

Lab 09 then asks you to find every file in your group repository whose name contains `check`. In the expense-tracker after `uv sync`, `find . -name "*check*" -type f` prints 24 paths. Only two are outside `.venv`: the CI workflow, `./.github/workflows/check.yml`, and git's own `./.git/hooks/push-to-checkout.sample`, both inside hidden folders that plain `ls` never shows. The rest are mypy's own files, such as `checker.py`. Read the full path of each match, or start the search where you expect the file: `find .github -name "*check*"` prints only the workflow.
key_points: Everything is under `/`. No drive letters; on WSL the Windows disk is `/mnt/c`.
`~` is your home: `/home/alice` on Linux and WSL, `/Users/alice` on macOS.
`ls` hides names that start with a dot; `ls -a` shows them, plus `.` (this folder) and `..` (its parent).
`find` walks the whole tree from where you start it, hidden folders included.

sections.heading: Absolute and relative paths, and moving with cd
sections.body_md:
A path names a file by the folders you pass through to reach it. There are two kinds, and the first character tells you which (slide 10):

| Path | Means |
|---|---|
| `/home/alice/code/expense-tracker` | Absolute. Starts at `/`. Same from anywhere |
| `src/expense_tracker/cli.py` | Relative. Starts here |
| `../project-template` | Up one level, then down |
| `~/code` | Your home, then `code` |

"Here" means the current directory, the one `pwd` prints. A relative path is read from there, so the same relative path names different files in different places. `..` is one level up, so `../..` is two.

Lab 09 walks the expense-tracker with relative paths only:

```console
$ cd src/expense_tracker
$ pwd
/home/alice/code/expense-tracker/src/expense_tracker
$ cd ../../tests
$ pwd
/home/alice/code/expense-tracker/tests
$ cd ..
$ pwd
/home/alice/code/expense-tracker
```

`cd ../../tests` climbs two levels, to the project root, then goes down into `tests`. Then the lab uses absolute paths and shortcuts:

```console
$ cd ~/code
$ cd "$HOME/code/expense-tracker/src"
$ cd -
/home/alice/code
$ cd
$ pwd
/home/alice
```

`cd -` goes back to where you just were (and prints it). `cd` alone goes home. `echo $HOME` prints `/home/alice`, the same as `pwd` right after a plain `cd`. These answer lab 09's questions 3 and 4.

The lab's path questions, for alice: the absolute path of `report.py` is `/home/alice/code/expense-tracker/src/expense_tracker/report.py`. The relative path from the project root is `src/expense_tracker/report.py`; from `tests` it is `../src/expense_tracker/report.py`; from `~` it is `code/expense-tracker/src/expense_tracker/report.py`.

Two spellings catch people out. The project's name uses a hyphen (`expense-tracker`: the repository, and the `name` in `pyproject.toml`); the Python package uses an underscore (`expense_tracker`, the folder under `src/`). These are the two spellings session 5 set up, because Python names cannot contain hyphens. A path has to match the real name character for character.
key_points: Absolute paths start at `/` and mean the same file from anywhere. Relative paths start here.
`..` is one level up; `cd -` goes back to where you just were; `cd` alone goes home.
From the project root, `report.py` is `src/expense_tracker/report.py`; from `tests`, `../src/expense_tracker/report.py`.

sections.heading: Reading a path in an error
sections.body_md:
Slide 10's rule: most "file not found" errors are the wrong current directory. Run `pwd` first.

A program reads a relative path from the folder you are standing in, not from the folder where its code lives. Here alice is in `tests` and asks for `expenses.csv`:

```console
$ pwd
/home/alice/code/expense-tracker/tests
$ uv run expenses report expenses.csv
could not read expenses.csv
$ echo $?
1
$ ls expenses.csv
ls: cannot access 'expenses.csv': No such file or directory
$ cd ..
$ uv run expenses report expenses.csv
Expense report for expenses.csv
----------------------------------------
groceries              6401.78
```

Slide 11 asks: which `expenses.csv`? The one in the folder you are standing in, not the one next to the code. `uv run` found the project (it looks upwards for `pyproject.toml`), but the program then opened `tests/expenses.csv`, which does not exist. The message and the exit code 1 are the program failing well (session 7): it names what it could not read. Your job is to read that path against `pwd`. Nothing is broken and nothing needs reinstalling. Either stand in the right folder, or give a path that is right from where you are, such as `../expenses.csv`.

Slide 11 itself shows the opposite slip: `pwd` prints `/home/alice/code`, one level too high, `ls expenses.csv` says `cannot access`, and `cd expense-tracker` fixes it. Too high or too deep, the diagnosis is the same: read the path against `pwd`.

The same rule applies to files a program writes. `expenses add` writes to `data/expenses.csv`, a relative path, so running it from `tests` creates `tests/data/expenses.csv`.

Slide 12's time savers also keep you out of wrong paths:

- **Tab** completes names. If it does not complete, the name is wrong or ambiguous. Treat it as a check, not only as less typing.
- **↑** brings back the last command, so you change one word instead of retyping the line.
- **Ctrl-R** searches your history for an older command.
- **Ctrl-C** stops the program that is running.
- **`cd -`** goes back to where you just were; **`cd`** alone goes home.
key_points: Most "file not found" errors are the wrong current directory. Run `pwd` first.
A relative path in an error is relative to where you stand, not to where the code is.
If Tab does not complete a name, the name is wrong or ambiguous.
Ctrl-C stops the running program; Ctrl-R searches your history.
sections.exam_note_md: The teacher's distractors for this transcript are the careless reflexes: reinstall, `chmod 777`, edit the code. The right move is always `pwd`, then the right folder.

sections.heading: Make, copy, move, remove
sections.body_md:
Five commands manage files. Slide 14 runs them in order:

```console
$ mkdir notes
$ touch notes/todo.txt
$ cp notes/todo.txt notes/todo-backup.txt
$ cp -r notes notes-old
$ mv notes/todo-backup.txt notes/old.txt
$ rm notes/old.txt
```

- `mkdir` makes a folder; `touch` makes an empty file.
- `cp` copies a file. `cp -r` copies a folder and everything in it.
- `mv` moves, and is also rename: moving a file to a new name renames it.
- `rm` removes. It does not ask and there is no bin. What it removes is gone.

After those six lines, `notes` holds only `todo.txt`, and `notes-old` holds `todo-backup.txt` and `todo.txt`: `cp -r` copied the folder as it was at that moment, and the later `mv` and `rm` only touched `notes`.

Without `-r`, `cp` refuses a folder and copies nothing:

```console
$ cp reports reports-copy
cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'reports'
```

`mv` follows one rule with two outcomes. If the target is an existing folder, the file goes inside it. If it is not, the target becomes the new name. So `mv reports/notes.txt reports/2025`, when `reports/2025` does not exist, silently turns `notes.txt` into a file called `2025`. Writing the folder with a trailing slash (`reports/2025/`), as in the table below, makes `mv` refuse with an error instead.

Lab 09, exercise 2, one command per task (in `~/lab09`):

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Copy `expenses.csv` into `reports/archive/` as `expenses-backup.csv` | `cp reports/expenses.csv reports/archive/expenses-backup.csv` |
| Move `notes.txt` into `reports/2025/` | `mv reports/notes.txt reports/2025/` |
| Rename it to `summary.txt` | `mv reports/2025/notes.txt reports/2025/summary.txt` |
| Copy the whole `reports` folder | `cp -r reports reports-copy` |

Then the part with no undo: after `rm -r reports-copy`, `ls reports-copy` says `ls: cannot access 'reports-copy': No such file or directory`, and there is no bin to get it back from.

The lab's habit for data: never edit `expenses.csv` in place, because it is a fixture the course relies on. Copy it, then work on the copy.
key_points: `mv` is also rename. `cp -r` copies a folder and everything in it.
`rm` does not ask and there is no bin. What it removes is gone.
`mv` into a folder that does not exist renames instead of moving.
Copy the data, never edit the original.

sections.heading: rm is permanent: the space and the star
sections.body_md:
Slide 15 shows two lines that differ by one space:

```console
$ rm -r notes-old
$ rm -r notes-old/ *
```

The first removes the folder `notes-old`. The second removes `notes-old/` and every file in the current directory. Two things combine.

**The space splits arguments.** The shell cuts the line into words at spaces. `notes-old/*` is one argument (everything inside `notes-old`); `notes-old/ *` is two: the folder, and a separate `*`.

**The shell expands `*` before `rm` runs.** `*` stands for every name in the current folder, except names that start with a dot. `rm` never sees the star; it receives the list. With `-r`, folders in that list go too.

Lab 09 asks you to reason out `rm -r reports-copy *` typed in `~/lab09`, where `ls` shows `reports  reports-copy`. The shell turns it into `rm -r reports-copy reports reports-copy`. `rm` removes `reports-copy`, then `reports` with everything in it, then complains that `reports-copy` is no longer there:

```console
$ rm -r reports-copy *
rm: cannot remove 'reports-copy': No such file or directory
$ ls
$ ls -a
.  ..
```

The only message looks like a failure, but the damage is done and the folder is empty. In a project folder, `.git`, `.github` and `.gitignore` would survive, because `*` skips dot names, while `src`, `tests` and `pyproject.toml` would not. Whatever you had pushed can be cloned again from GitHub; uncommitted work is gone.

The slide's habits:

- `ls` the exact path before you `rm` it. Then press ↑ and swap `ls` for `rm`, so what you checked is exactly what you delete.
- `rm -i` asks first. Use it when you are tired.
- Never `rm -rf` with a variable you have not printed. An empty variable turns `rm -rf "$DIR/"*` into `rm -rf /*`.
key_points: The shell expands `*` to every name here before `rm` runs; `rm` never sees the star.
A space turns one argument into two: `notes-old/*` is not `notes-old/ *`.
`ls` the exact path first, then press ↑ and swap `ls` for `rm`.
`rm -i` asks first; never `rm -rf` with a variable you have not printed.

sections.heading: Reading permissions in ls -l
sections.body_md:
`ls -l` prints one line per entry (slide 17):

```console
$ ls -l
-rw-rw-r-- 1 alice alice  1193 Oct 11 17:07 README.md
-rw-rw-r-- 1 alice alice 15221 Oct 11 17:07 expenses.csv
drwxrwxr-x 3 alice alice    60 Oct 11 17:07 src
```

Left to right: the type and permissions, a link count you can ignore, the owner, the group, the size in bytes, the date of the last change, and the name.

On a Mac, `ls -l` may show an `@` after the permission letters (`-rw-r--r--@`). Lab 09 says it marks extended attributes; ignore it. The listings in this module follow the slide's Linux format.

The first ten characters are the part to read carefully:

```text
-  rw-  rw-  r--
d  rwx  rwx  r-x
│   │    │    └── everyone else
│   │    └─────── your group
│   └──────────── you (the owner)
└──────────────── type: - file, d directory
```

The first character is the type: `-` for a file, `d` for a directory. That answers lab 09's question "which entries are folders?" without guessing from names or sizes. Then come three groups of three, always in the order owner, group, everyone else. In each group, `r` is read, `w` is write and `x` is execute; a `-` means that permission is missing.

For a folder, `x` means you may enter it. Without `x`, even the owner cannot go in or reach the files inside, whatever `r` and `w` say:

```console
$ ls -ld reports
drw-rw-r-- 2 alice alice 4096 Oct 13 10:12 reports
$ cd reports
bash: cd: reports: Permission denied
$ cat reports/notes.txt
cat: reports/notes.txt: Permission denied
```

So the slide's listing says: alice (the owner) and members of the group `alice` can read and write `README.md` and `expenses.csv`; everyone else can only read them; nobody can execute them. `src` is a folder everyone may enter. On Ubuntu each user gets a group of their own, which is why owner and group are both `alice`.

When a question shows `ls -l` output, read the first character, then the three groups, then answer what the scenario cares about: who can change this, and can it be run?
key_points: First character: `-` file, `d` directory. Then owner, group, everyone else, three letters each.
`r` read, `w` write, `x` execute; for a folder, `x` means you can enter it.
Read the line for the question asked: who can change it, and can it run?
sections.exam_note_md: Listings in questions are in GNU format, like the slide's. Read the first character before anything else.

sections.heading: Permission denied: chmod +x, ./ and PATH
sections.body_md:
Slides 18–19 are the session's most common surprise:

```console
$ cat hello.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo hello
$ ./hello.sh
permission denied: ./hello.sh
$ ls -l hello.sh
-rw-rw-r-- 1 alice alice 31 Oct 11 17:07 hello.sh
```

There is no `x`. Nobody said this file is a program. A new file never gets execution permissions, whether you make it with `touch`, with `printf ... > run.sh` as lab 09 does, or in VS Code. The fix is to say it:

```console
$ chmod +x hello.sh
$ ls -l hello.sh
-rwxrwxr-x 1 alice alice 31 Oct 11 17:07 hello.sh
$ ./hello.sh
hello
```

`chmod +x` is a statement that a file is a program. (The slide's message comes from `zsh`; `bash` says `bash: ./hello.sh: Permission denied`.)

**Why `./`?** `./` means "this folder": run the `hello.sh` that is here. Without it, the shell does not look in the current folder; it searches the folders listed in `PATH` (where `uv`, `git` and `ls` live). Lab 09 makes you try it: after `chmod +x run.sh`, `./run.sh` prints `report ready`, but a bare `run.sh` gives `run.sh: command not found` (plain `bash`, without Ubuntu's helper, prints `bash: run.sh: command not found`).

**`bash run.sh` is a different thing.** It starts `bash` and hands it the file to read, so it needs only `r`; it is how session 3's `bash scripts/setup-check.sh` runs, with or without `x`. `./run.sh` asks to run the file itself, and that needs `x`. Slide 20 assumes the second way: a CI step that runs `./scripts/check.sh` needs the bit committed.

**Not every file should be a program.** In the expense-tracker, `ls -l src/expense_tracker` shows `__init__.py`, `cli.py` and `report.py` without `x`: none can be run directly. That is right for Python modules: the package imports them, and importing only needs `r`. The program is `expenses`, which uv builds from `[project.scripts]` into `.venv/bin` with the `x` bit set; `uv run expenses` runs that.

**Where chmod does nothing.** On WSL, a project under `/mnt/c` shows every file as `rwxrwxrwx`, and `chmod` silently does nothing. Keep projects in your Linux home, `~/code/...` (the same reason `uv` and `git` are faster there). Check: `pwd` should start with `/home/`, not `/mnt/`.

**CI needs the bit too.** Friday's `scripts/check.sh` depends on this: in CI it needs the `x` bit, and git remembers it. After `chmod +x scripts/check.sh`, `git diff` shows `old mode 100644` and `new mode 100755`; you commit and push that like any other change, and every fresh clone, CI's included, gets a runnable script.
key_points: No `x`, no run. `chmod +x` is a statement that a file is a program.
A new file never gets execute permission.
`./` means this folder; without it the shell only searches `PATH`.
On WSL, `chmod` silently does nothing under `/mnt/c`: keep projects in `~/code`.
git remembers the `x` bit, and CI needs it on `scripts/check.sh`.

sections.heading: Numbers instead of letters: 644, 755, 600, 777
sections.body_md:
`chmod` also takes numbers. r = 4, w = 2, x = 1. Add them per group of three, in the usual order owner, group, everyone else (slide 21):

| Number | Letters | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| 644 | `rw-r--r--` | A normal file |
| 755 | `rwxr-xr-x` | A script or a folder |
| 600 | `rw-------` | A private key |
| 777 | `rwxrwxrwx` | Almost never the answer |

So `rwxr-xr-x` is 4+2+1, 4+1, 4+1 = 755, and `rw-------` is 4+2, 0, 0 = 600: lab 09's question 4.

Each row is a judgement about who needs what. A normal file: you edit it, others may read it, nobody runs it. A script or a folder: everyone may run or enter it, only you change it. A private key: nobody but you may even read it; `ssh-keygen` creates `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` as 600 for that reason, and `ssh` refuses a private key that others can read.

Lab 09 then sets 600 on the script:

```console
$ chmod 600 run.sh
$ ls -l run.sh
-rw------- 1 alice alice 40 Oct 13 10:12 run.sh
$ ./run.sh
bash: ./run.sh: Permission denied
$ cat run.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "report ready"
```

You can no longer run it (no `x`), but you can still read it with `cat` (the owner kept `r`).

**Why 777 is almost never the answer.** `chmod 777` makes the error go away and the problem worse. "Permission denied" on a script means one bit is missing, the `x`. 777 adds it, and also gives every user on the machine permission to change the file. On a script that CI runs, or a key that proves who you are, that is the opposite of what you want. Add the one bit that is missing (`chmod +x`, or 755) and nothing else.

**A few more tools.** `man ls` opens the manual (`q` quits) and `ls --help` is shorter. `whoami`, `date`, `uname -a`, `df -h`, `top` and `nano` exist too. The slide is plain about them: you may look these up when they are needed; they are not examined as recall. The mid-term asks what a command does in a scenario, never what a letter stands for.
key_points: 644 a normal file, 755 a script or folder, 600 a private key.
`chmod 777` makes the error go away and the problem worse.
`man` and `--help` exist so you do not have to memorise flags.
sections.exam_note_md: Conversions come inside a judgement: which number fits this file, and why the tempting one (777, or 600 on a script) is wrong.

What actually creates files and starts programs. On WSL and Linux, the Linux kernel.
The top of the one tree that holds every file. Absolute paths start there. There are no drive letters.
Your own folder: `/home/alice` on Linux and WSL, `/Users/alice` on macOS. `~` and `$HOME` both mean it, and `cd` alone goes there.
Where WSL shows your Windows C: drive. `git` and `uv` are slow there and `chmod` silently does nothing; keep projects in `~/code`.
A name that starts with a dot, such as `.git` or `.github`. `ls` hides it, `ls -a` shows it, and `*` does not match it.
`.` is the folder you are in; `..` is its parent. `./run.sh` means the `run.sh` in this folder.
The folder you are standing in, printed by `pwd`. Relative paths are read from it, for reading and for writing.
A path that starts at `/`, such as `/home/alice/code/expense-tracker`. It names the same file from anywhere.
A path that starts here, such as `src/expense_tracker/cli.py` or `../tests`. What it names depends on the current directory.
Tab completes a file or folder name as you type. If it does not complete, the name is wrong or ambiguous.

On its own, `*` stands for every name in the current folder except names that start with a dot; `notes-old/*` stands for every name inside `notes-old`. The shell expands it into a list before the command runs.
The first ten characters of an `ls -l` line: the type (`-` file, `d` directory), then `r`, `w`, `x` for the owner, the group and everyone else.
On a file: it may be run as a program. On a folder: you may enter it. A new file never gets it.
Changes permissions, with letters (`chmod +x run.sh`) or numbers (`chmod 755 run.sh`).
The list of folders the shell searches for a command typed without a path. The current folder is not in it, which is why you type `./run.sh`.
git records whether a file is executable (`100755`) or not (`100644`). A fresh clone, CI's included, gets the mode that was committed.
Permissions as three digits, one per group, with r = 4, w = 2, x = 1: 644, 755, 600, 777.

traps: "The terminal runs my script." The terminal is only the window. The shell (`bash`, `zsh`) reads and runs your line, and the operating system creates files and starts programs.
"There is no `.git`, so the clone is broken." `ls` hides names that start with a dot; `ls -a` shows `.git`.
"File not found means the file is missing or the program is broken." Most of the time you are in the wrong folder: relative paths are read from where you stand. Run `pwd` first.
"A program reads files from the folder its code is in." It reads (and writes) relative paths from the current directory: `expenses add` run in `tests` creates `tests/data/expenses.csv`.
"`rm -r old *` only removes `old`." The space makes `*` its own argument, and the shell expands it to every name in the folder before `rm` runs.
"I can get it back from the bin." `rm` has no bin and no undo. Only your own copy or a committed version brings it back.
"Permission denied, so `chmod 777`." Only the `x` was missing. 777 also gives everyone write permission: it makes the error go away and the problem worse.
"`run.sh` is right here, so typing `run.sh` should run it." Without `./`, the shell only searches the folders in `PATH`, and the current folder is not one of them.
"No error, so `chmod` worked." Under `/mnt/c` on WSL, `chmod` silently does nothing. Check with `ls -l`, and keep projects in `~/code`.
"It runs on my laptop, so it runs in CI." CI clones what git recorded. If the `x` bit of `scripts/check.sh` was never committed, CI says Permission denied.
"`bash run.sh` works, so the `x` bit does not matter." `bash run.sh` only reads the file, which needs `r`. Running it by its own name, as CI runs `./scripts/check.sh`, needs `x`.

categories.label: Shell (reads the line and runs it)

items.text_md: Windows Terminal, or GNOME Terminal
items.why_md: Window programs: they show text and send your keystrokes, and you can swap one for another.

items.text_md: `bash` on WSL's Ubuntu
items.why_md: `bash` is the program that reads each line you type and runs it.

items.text_md: `zsh`, the default on every recent macOS
items.why_md: Another shell. It is why lab 00 sends Mac users to `~/.zshrc` rather than `~/.bashrc`.

items.text_md: The Linux kernel
items.why_md: The slide's example of the operating system: what actually creates files and starts programs.

items.why_md: Cutting the line into arguments and expanding `*` happen in the shell, before any program runs.

items.text_md: Actually creates `notes/todo.txt` on the disk when `touch` asks for it
items.why_md: `touch` asks the operating system to create the file; neither the window nor the shell writes to the disk itself.

items.text_md: Shows text and sends your keystrokes

questions.explanation_md: The slide's table has three rows. The terminal is the window (Windows Terminal, GNOME Terminal). The shell is the program inside it that reads a line and runs it (`bash` on WSL and Linux, `zsh` on macOS). The operating system is what actually creates files and starts programs (the Linux kernel). Two consequences follow. Terminal and shell swap independently, so changing the window changes nothing about your scripts. And anything that happens to your command line before a program starts, such as splitting it at spaces or expanding `*`, is the shell's doing.

questions.stem_md: Your group's `scripts/check.sh` starts with `#!/usr/bin/env bash`. A teammate on Windows replaces Windows Terminal with a different terminal app. Inside it she still opens WSL's Ubuntu, where `bash` runs as before. She asks whether the script needs changing. What do you tell her?

options.text_md: No. The terminal is only the window; the script depends on the shell, and that is still `bash`.
options.why_md: Right: terminal and shell swap independently, and scripts depend on the shell. Nothing that runs the script has changed.

options.text_md: Yes. Each terminal app runs scripts in its own way, so the script must be tested and adapted again.
options.why_md: This treats the window as the thing that runs commands. The terminal only shows text and sends keystrokes; the shell runs the script.

options.text_md: Yes. A new terminal app means a new operating system underneath, so file paths will be different.
options.why_md: The operating system is still WSL's Ubuntu with the Linux kernel. Changing the window changes neither the OS nor the tree under `/`.

options.text_md: No. Scripts depend only on the operating system, so neither the window nor the shell matters.
options.why_md: Right verdict, wrong reason. The slide says your scripts depend on the shell: a script written for `bash` can behave differently under another shell.

questions.explanation_md: Session 9 splits the everyday word "terminal" into three: the terminal (the window), the shell (the program that reads a line and runs it) and the operating system (what creates files and starts programs). The slide's conclusion is the one tested here: terminal and shell swap independently, and your scripts depend on the shell. Only the window changed. The shell is still `bash`, so `check.sh` behaves exactly as before. Option d reaches the same verdict with a reason that contradicts the slide; session 8's advice for checking your answers applies: judge your reasons, not the letter.

questions.stem_md: Before each push, a teammate runs the four checks by clicking buttons in VS Code's sidebar. He says writing them down as commands in `scripts/check.sh` is a waste of time. Which argument from session 9 answers him best?

questions.stem_md:
A teammate clones the group repository and runs `ls`:

```console
$ ls
LICENSE  README.md  pyproject.toml  scripts  src  tests  uv.lock
```

She messages you: "There is no `.git` folder, so the clone is broken. I'll run `git init`." What do you reply?

options.text_md: Run `git init`: a clone without a visible `.git` folder has no history, so it needs a new one.
options.why_md: The clone is fine. Acting on the symptom before checking the diagnosis is the careless move; the history is already there, hidden.

options.text_md: `.git` exists only on GitHub; her copy receives the history the first time she pushes.
options.why_md: `git clone` copies a repository down with its history (session 3's survival kit). The history lives in her local `.git`.

options.text_md: `.git` lives in her home folder and is shared by all the repositories she has cloned.
options.why_md: Each repository has its own `.git` inside its folder, as the slide's tree shows under `my-project/`.

options.text_md: `.git` is there, but hidden: `ls` hides names that start with a dot. `ls -a` will show it.
options.why_md: Right: `.git` starts with a dot, so `ls` hides it. That is why you never see it, and why it is safe.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 9: `ls` hides names that start with a dot. `.git` is one: that is why you never see it, and why it is safe. In the same folder, `ls -a` lists `.git`, `.github`, `.gitignore` and `.python-version` as well, plus `.` and `..`. The teammate's reasoning is the pattern the teacher's distractors are built on: a symptom (nothing visible) is read as a broken tool, and a fix is applied before the diagnosis is checked. One extra command, `ls -a`, settles it.

questions.stem_md:
In lab 09's stretch exercise, alice runs `find` in a fresh clone of the expense-tracker where she has only run `uv sync` so far. Its `tests` folder holds three test files:

```console
$ find . -name "test_*" -type f | wc -l
44
$ find . -name "test_*" -type f | head -5
./tests/test_report.py
./tests/test_io.py
./tests/test_duplicates.py
./.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/mypyc/test/test_pprint.py
./.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/mypyc/test/test_rarray.py
```

Why 44 and not 3?

options.text_md: `find` counts every test function inside the matching files, not the files themselves.
options.why_md: `find` matches names in the tree and never opens files. Each line of its output is one path.

options.text_md: From `.`, `find` also walked into the hidden `.venv`, where installed packages ship test files.
options.why_md: Right: the extra paths are under `./.venv/lib/...`. Unlike `ls`, `find` does not skip names that start with a dot.

options.text_md: `find` also searched the old versions of each test file that git keeps inside the hidden `.git` folder.
options.why_md: git stores old versions under hashed object names, not as `test_*.py` files, and none of the paths shown is under `.git`.

options.text_md: `tests/` holds 41 hidden copies of the test files, which plain `ls` never shows.
options.why_md: A hidden copy would start with a dot, so it could not match `test_*`; the extra paths shown are under `./.venv`.

questions.explanation_md: `find` searches a tree, starting from the folder you give it; `.` is the folder you are in. It does not hide dot names the way `ls` does, so it walks into `.venv`, the virtual environment uv created, where mypy and mypyc ship their own test files whose names match `test_*`. Lab 09's exercise 4 is about exactly this: a name repeats across the tree, and the full path is what tells two files apart. To count only the project's tests, start where they live and match the source files: `find tests -name "test_*.py" -type f` prints the three. After `uv run pytest`, `tests/__pycache__` also holds compiled copies named `test_*.pyc`, which the bare `"test_*"` pattern would count.

questions.stem_md:
alice types these five commands, one after another:

```bash
cd ~/code/expense-tracker/src/expense_tracker
cd ../../tests
cd -
cd ..
pwd
```

What does the last one print?

options.text_md: `/home/alice/code/expense-tracker/src`
options.why_md: Right: `cd -` returns to `src/expense_tracker`, and `cd ..` then goes up one level, to `src`.

options.text_md: `/home/alice/code/expense-tracker`
options.why_md: This skips the `cd -`: from `tests`, `cd ..` would reach the project root. But `cd -` first went back to `src/expense_tracker`.

options.text_md: `/home/alice/code`
options.why_md: This reads `cd -` as "up one level", like `cd ..`. `cd -` goes back to where you just were.

options.text_md: `/home`
options.why_md: This reads `cd -` as "go home" (that is `cd` alone) and then goes up one level from `/home/alice`.

questions.explanation_md: Track `pwd` line by line. The first `cd` lands in `/home/alice/code/expense-tracker/src/expense_tracker`. `cd ../../tests` climbs two levels to the project root and goes down into `tests`. `cd -` goes back to where you just were, `src/expense_tracker` (bash prints that path as it goes). `cd ..` goes up one level, to `/home/alice/code/expense-tracker/src`. Each wrong option comes from misreading a single shortcut: ignoring `cd -`, taking it for `cd ..`, or taking it for `cd` alone.

questions.stem_md: Which of these paths names the expense-tracker's `report.py` the same way whatever the current directory is?

options.text_md: `src/expense_tracker/report.py`
options.why_md: Relative: it starts here, so it only works from the project root.

options.text_md: `../expense-tracker/src/expense_tracker/report.py`
options.why_md: Relative: it only works from a folder directly inside `~/code`, such as `~/code/flashcard-trainer`.

options.text_md: `code/expense-tracker/src/expense_tracker/report.py`
options.why_md: Relative: it only works from alice's home folder, `/home/alice`.

options.text_md: `/home/alice/code/expense-tracker/src/expense_tracker/report.py`
options.why_md: Right: it starts at `/`, so it is absolute and means the same file from anywhere.

questions.explanation_md: The first character decides. A path that starts with `/` is absolute: it is read from the root of the one tree, so it names the same file from any current directory. Every other path here is relative: it starts here, from the folder `pwd` prints, so it names `report.py` only from certain places (the project root, a folder directly inside `~/code`, or the home folder). All three relative paths are correct somewhere, which is exactly why none is correct everywhere.
questions.source_ref: S9 slide 10; labs/09-terminal.md ('What done looks like' Q2)

questions.stem_md: alice is in `/home/alice/code/expense-tracker/tests` and wants to look at `report.py` without moving. Which path reaches `src/expense_tracker/report.py` from where she stands?

options.text_md: `src/expense_tracker/report.py`
options.why_md: That is the path from the project root. From `tests` it points to `tests/src/...`, which does not exist.

options.text_md: `../src/expense_tracker/report.py`
options.why_md: Right: `..` goes up from `tests` to the project root, then the path goes down into `src`.

options.text_md: `/src/expense_tracker/report.py`
options.why_md: A leading `/` starts at the root of the whole tree, not at the project, and there is no `/src` folder.

options.text_md: `../../src/expense_tracker/report.py`

options.text_md: From `~/code/expense-tracker`: `README.md`. From `~/code/flashcard-trainer`: `README.md`.
options.why_md: Same text, different starting folders: these are the two projects' own READMEs.

options.why_md: The first is the expense-tracker's README; the second would be `/home/alice/README.md`, which does not exist.

options.text_md: From `~/code/flashcard-trainer`: `../expense-tracker/README.md`. From `~`: `code/expense-tracker/README.md`.
options.why_md: Right: both resolve to `/home/alice/code/expense-tracker/README.md`.

options.text_md: From `~`: `code/expense-tracker/README.md`. From `~/code/expense-tracker`: `code/expense-tracker/README.md`.

options.why_md: A dot at the start of a name hides it; `./` is a path meaning this folder, not part of the name.

options.text_md: The shell runs `.sh` files only when you type `bash` in front of the name.
options.why_md: `./run.sh` ran a moment earlier with no `bash` in front of it.

questions.explanation_md: Lab 09 asks this directly: what does `./` in front of the name mean, and why does `run.sh` alone fail? `./` means "this folder", so `./run.sh` is a path to the file here. A bare name is looked up as a command in the folders listed in `PATH`, which is how `uv`, `git` and `ls` are found. The current folder is not in `PATH`, so the shell reports `command not found`. That protects you: a file lying in whatever folder you happen to be in does not run just because its name matches a command.

If it only looked executable on your machine (under `/mnt/c` everything shows `rwxrwxrwx`), or you ran `chmod +x` but never committed it, CI's copy has no `x`. The local run proves nothing about what git recorded. A real run of the same step on a fresh clone without the bit produces the log line above; after `chmod +x` in a Linux folder and a commit, `git diff` shows `old mode 100644` / `new mode 100755`, and a fresh clone has the `x` bit. When git finds that `chmod` has no effect, as under `/mnt/c`, it sets `core.fileMode` to `false` and stops trusting the `x` bits it sees; a real run with that setting records a `rwxrwxrwx` file as `100644`.

questions.stem_md:
```console
$ chmod 600 run.sh
$ ls -l run.sh
-rw------- 1 alice alice 40 Oct 13 10:12 run.sh
```

Lab 09 asks what alice can now do. What happens with `./run.sh` and with `cat run.sh`?

options.text_md: Both work: 600 only restricts the other users, never the owner.
options.why_md: The owner's letters are `rw-`: no `x`, so even alice cannot run it.

options.text_md: Neither works: 600 locks the file completely until it is changed back.
options.why_md: The owner keeps `r` and `w`, so reading and editing still work.

options.text_md: `./run.sh` says Permission denied; `cat run.sh` still prints the script.
options.why_md: Right: 6 is `rw-` (4 + 2), with no 1 for execute, and alice kept `r`.

options.text_md: `./run.sh` works because alice owns it; `cat run.sh` fails because the group lost `r`.
options.why_md: Owning a file does not make it runnable, and `cat` run by alice uses the owner's letters, which include `r`.

questions.explanation_md: Turn the number back into letters per group of three: 6 = 4 + 2 = `rw-` for the owner, 0 = `---` for the group, 0 = `---` for everyone else. That is slide 21's private-key setting: only the owner can read and write. Without `x`, the shell refuses to run the script; with `r`, `cat` reads it. The real run shows `bash: ./run.sh: Permission denied`, then the two lines of the script from `cat`.

questions.stem_md: After "Permission denied" on `scripts/check.sh`, a teammate ran `chmod 777 scripts/check.sh`, saw the script run, and wants to close the issue. Which review comment is right?

options.text_md: Fine: 777 is the standard setting for scripts, so nothing else is needed here.
options.why_md: The slide's setting for a script is 755; 777 is "almost never the answer".

options.text_md: Use 600 instead: a script should be private, like an SSH key.
options.why_md: 600 has no `x` at all: the script would be denied again, and CI could not run it.

options.text_md: Use 644 instead: scripts kept in a repository should never be executable.
options.why_md: 644 is a normal file with no `x`, so `./scripts/check.sh` would fail again.

options.text_md: Use 755: only `x` was missing, and 777 lets anyone rewrite what CI runs.
options.why_md: Right: 755 is `rwxr-xr-x`, run by all, changed only by the owner; 777 gives every user write access to the script CI runs.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 21: `chmod 777` makes the error go away and the problem worse. "Permission denied" meant one thing: no `x`. 777 adds it, and also lets every user on the machine change the very script that decides whether CI is green. The right number adds only what was missing: 755 (`rwxr-xr-x`), or simply `chmod +x`. The other two numbers are real settings for other kinds of file: 600 for a private key, 644 for a normal file.

questions.stem_md: In a teammate's script you meet `cp -p` and do not know what `-p` does. What does session 9 suggest?

options.text_md: Read `man cp`, or the shorter `cp --help`: you look flags up when you need them.
options.why_md: Right: slide 22 lists `man` and `--help`, and says such details are not examined as recall.

options.text_md: Run the script on your real project and see what changes.
options.why_md: Lab 09's rule is to work on a copy; trying unknown commands on the original is how data gets lost.

options.text_md: Assume it means "path", since that is what `-p` means for most commands.
options.why_md: The same letter means different things in different commands; guessing is what the manual saves you from.

options.text_md: Delete `-p` from the script, since a flag you do not know cannot matter much.
options.why_md: Removing it changes what the script does, without knowing how.

Its last line is the important one: you may look these up when they are needed; they are not examined as recall. The mid-term says the same: judgement, not memorised flags. What is examined is the judgement in this question: look it up, and never experiment on the original data.

questions.stem_md: Sort each file or folder into the permissions it should have, using slide 21's typical uses.

items.text_md: `README.md`
items.why_md: A normal file: you edit it, others read it, nobody runs it.

items.text_md: `scripts/check.sh`, which CI runs as `./scripts/check.sh`
items.why_md: A script: everyone may run it, only the owner changes it.

items.text_md: `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, your private SSH key
items.why_md: A private key: nobody but you may even read it, and `ssh` refuses it otherwise.

items.text_md: `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`, the key you pasted into GitHub
items.why_md: The public half is meant to be shared, so others may read it.

items.text_md: The `src/` folder
items.why_md: A folder needs `x` to be entered; 755 allows everyone in and only you to change it.

items.text_md: `expenses.csv`, the sample data
items.why_md: Data, not a program: read by all, written by you.

items.text_md: `src/expense_tracker/report.py`
items.why_md: A module the package imports, not a program, so no `x`.

items.text_md: The `tests/` folder
items.why_md: Like every folder, it needs `x` so that you, and pytest, can enter it.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 21 pairs each number with a typical use: 644 a normal file, 755 a script or a folder, 600 a private key, 777 almost never. For each item ask two questions. Does it run, or is it a folder? Then it needs `x`: 755. Must others not even read it? Then 600. Everything else is a normal file: 644. On Ubuntu your own files often show as `rw-rw-r--` (664) and folders as `rwxrwxr-x` (775), because your group is just you; the judgement is the same.

questions.stem_md:
alice copies her SSH key from her old laptop with a USB stick. The next time she connects to GitHub, the output starts with these lines:

```text
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
@         WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!          @
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
Permissions 0644 for '/home/alice/.ssh/id_ed25519' are too open.
It is required that your private key files are NOT accessible by others.
This private key will be ignored.
Load key "/home/alice/.ssh/id_ed25519": bad permissions
```

parts.prompt_md: What is ssh complaining about? Write `0644` as letters and say who can do what.
parts.model_answer_md: 644 is `rw-r--r--`: alice can read and write the key, and her group and everyone else can read it. A private key is what proves she is alice, so ssh refuses to use one that other users can read.
rubric: Translates 644 into `rw-r--r--` (owner read and write, group and others read)
Explains that others can read the private key, so ssh ignores it
parts.weak_answers_md: "The key is broken" ignores the message, which names the permissions. Translating 644 as "read, write, execute" mixes up the arithmetic: 6 is 4 + 2, read and write, and 4 is read only. "The permissions are wrong" without saying who can read the key misses the point of the warning.

parts.prompt_md: Which permissions should the file have, as a number and in letters, and why not 755?
parts.model_answer_md: 600, `rw-------`: only alice can read and write it. Not 755: a key is not a program, so it needs no `x`, and 755 would still let everyone read it.
rubric: 600 / `rw-------` (owner only)
Rejects 755: a key needs no `x`, and 755 still allows group and others to read it
parts.weak_answers_md: Answering 700 or 755 "to be safe" adds an `x` that a key never needs, and 755 keeps it readable by others. Giving the number without the letters, or the letters without saying whom they apply to, earns half.

parts.prompt_md: Her friend says: "just `chmod 777` it so ssh stops complaining". What happens?
parts.model_answer_md: It makes things worse: with 777 everyone can read and change the key, and ssh still refuses it, now saying `Permissions 0777 ... are too open`.
rubric: 777 is more open, not less: ssh still refuses the key, and everyone could read and change it
parts.weak_answers_md: "777 gives ssh permission" misreads the warning: ssh refuses because others have access, so more access cannot fix it. This is slide 21's line in a new place: 777 makes the problem worse, and here it does not even make the error go away.

questions.explanation_md: A small step beyond the slides, using only their table: slide 21 lists 600 as the typical use for a private key, and this is what happens when the rule is broken. `ssh-keygen` (lab 00) creates the key as 600 and the `.pub` file as 644; copying a key from a USB stick is a typical way to lose the 600. A real run shows this warning for 0644, the same refusal for 0777, and the key loading normally again after `chmod 600`.

questions.stem_md:
Before tagging v0.5, Ben runs `chmod +x scripts/check.sh` in the group repository, in his Linux home, and looks at what git sees:

```console
$ git status --short
 M scripts/check.sh
$ git diff
diff --git a/scripts/check.sh b/scripts/check.sh
old mode 100644
new mode 100755
```

He offers two commit messages:

- A: `fix ci`
- B: `Make scripts/check.sh executable so CI can run it`

parts.prompt_md: What does this change do, and why does git call the file modified when no line of it changed?
parts.model_answer_md: It makes the script executable: git's record of the file goes from 644, a normal file, to 755, a script, so `./scripts/check.sh` can run. git records each file's mode as well as its lines, so the mode change is a modification, and every fresh clone, CI's included, gets it.
rubric: Says the script becomes executable: mode 644 to 755, the `x` bit added, so `./scripts/check.sh` can run
Says git records the file mode as well as the content, so the change shows as modified and reaches every clone, CI's included
parts.weak_answers_md: "Nothing changed, the diff is empty" misses the two mode lines: the `x` bit is the change. "Now everyone can edit the script" misreads 755: only the owner has `w`. "It makes the script run as administrator" confuses execute permission with a different user. Saying only "it changes permissions", without naming the `x` bit or saying that git stores it, earns half.

parts.prompt_md: Which message is better for someone reading the history six months later, and why?
parts.model_answer_md: B. It names the file, the change and the reason, so a reader of `git log` knows what happened without opening the diff. A names neither file nor change, and the diff has no changed lines, so the commit could pass for empty.
rubric: Chooses B because it says what changed (which file, made executable) and why (so CI can run it)
Says A is vague: no file and no change, so the reader must open the diff, where a mode-only change looks empty
parts.weak_answers_md: "B, because it is longer" gives no reason: the point is what the message tells the reader, not its length. "A is fine because the team knows what it means" forgets the reader six months later, who was not there. Choosing B without saying what A fails to tell the reader earns one mark.

parts.prompt_md: Name one check, in words, that shows the change worked before you tag v0.5.
parts.model_answer_md: Push and check that CI's step running `./scripts/check.sh` no longer says Permission denied, or clone the repository into a new folder and see the `x` with `ls -l`.
rubric: A check on a fresh copy, not his own folder: the CI run on the pushed commit, or a fresh clone in the Linux home showing `x` on the script
parts.weak_answers_md: "Run it again on my laptop" proves nothing about what git recorded: his own copy already has the bit, committed or not. "Write a test for it" is too vague to mark: say what you would run and what you expect to see.

questions.explanation_md: The compare shape of sample Q8, applied to session 9. A diff can change something other than lines: `old mode 100644` / `new mode 100755` is git recording that `scripts/check.sh` became executable, and the last three digits are slide 21's numbers (644 a normal file, 755 a script). Slide 20 says why it matters: in CI the script needs the `x` bit, and git remembers it. A good message says what the change does and why, which matters most when the diff itself looks empty. The check has to look at a fresh copy, because CI does not use your folder: it clones what git recorded. A real run gives the same `git status` and `git diff` output, and a fresh clone of the commit has the `x` bit.

questions.stem_md: Each line is the first error a student saw, with what they had just done. Sort each one by what is really wrong.

categories.label: A file and a folder mixed up

items.text_md: `could not read expenses.csv`, just after `pwd` printed `/home/alice/code/expense-tracker/tests`
items.why_md: The relative name was read from `tests`; the file is in the project root.

items.text_md: `bash: cd: expense-tracker: No such file or directory`, just after `pwd` printed `/home/alice`
items.why_md: The project is inside `~/code`, so from home the relative name points nowhere.

items.text_md: `bash: ./run.sh: Permission denied`, where `ls -l run.sh` shows `-rw-rw-r--`
items.why_md: No `x` in any group: nobody has said this file is a program.

items.text_md: `bash: cd: reports: Permission denied`, where `ls -ld reports` shows `drw-rw-r--`
items.why_md: For a folder, `x` means enter it, and even the owner has none.

items.why_md: The file runs, so nothing is missing from it; without `./` the shell only searches the folders in `PATH`.

items.text_md: `bash: cd: reports/2025: Not a directory`, after `mv reports/notes.txt reports/2025`
items.why_md: No folder `2025` existed, so `mv` renamed the file to `2025`, and `cd` was then asked to enter a file.

questions.explanation_md: Session 9's errors fall into a few kinds, and each kind has its own fix. Two lines that both end in `Permission denied`, or two that both say a name is missing, can mean different things, so read the path in the error against what happened just before it: `pwd`, `ls -l`, or the previous command. Wrong folder: move, or give a path that is right from where you stand. No `x`: `chmod +x` in your Linux home, committed for CI, never 777. Not in `PATH`: type `./`. File and folder mixed up: `cp -r` for a folder, and `ls` before `mv`, which renames when the target folder does not exist. Every line here comes from a real run shown elsewhere in this module.

questions.stem_md:
```console
$ ls -l run.sh
-rw-rw-r-- 1 alice alice 40 Oct 13 10:12 run.sh
$ ./run.sh
bash: ./run.sh: Permission denied
$ bash run.sh
report ready
```

A teammate concludes that the `x` bit is pointless, since `bash run.sh` works without it. What is the best reply?

options.text_md: `bash` ignores permissions on every file, so it can even run scripts that nobody may read.
options.why_md: `bash` still has to read the file. Once `r` is removed (`chmod 200 run.sh`, `--w-------`), `bash run.sh` is refused too: `bash: run.sh: Permission denied`.

options.text_md: `bash run.sh` runs `bash`, which only reads the file; `./run.sh` runs the file itself.
options.why_md: Right: reading needs `r`, which alice has; running the file as a program needs `x`, which nobody has.

options.text_md: `bash run.sh` quietly adds the `x` bit for one run, then takes it away again afterwards.
options.why_md: Nothing changes the mode: `ls -l` still shows `-rw-rw-r--`. Only `chmod` changes permissions.

options.text_md: He is right: in CI, `./scripts/check.sh` will also run without `x` if the file is readable.
options.why_md: `./scripts/check.sh` asks to run the file itself, which needs `x` on every machine. That is why slide 20 says CI needs the bit and git remembers it.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 19's rule, no `x`, no run, is about running a file as a program: `./run.sh` asks the operating system to start the file itself, and that needs `x`. `bash run.sh` starts a different program, `bash`, and gives it the file to read, which needs only `r`. It is also how session 3 and lab 00 run `bash scripts/setup-check.sh`, which works whether or not the file has `x`. The bit still matters whenever a script is run by its own name, as `./scripts/check.sh` is in CI. A real run confirms all of it: with `rw-rw-r--`, `./run.sh` is denied and `bash run.sh` prints `report ready`; after `chmod 200 run.sh`, `bash run.sh` is refused as well.

questions.stem_md: A teammate has to read a log file on a Linux server that the group rents. He connects with `ssh` and finds no desktop, no windows and no mouse, only a prompt. Which of session 9's reasons for the terminal explains why that prompt is all he gets?

options.text_md: It composes: small programs joined by pipes can answer any question about a log.
options.why_md: True of the terminal, but it does not explain why there is nothing else on the server. Composition is about how commands combine, not where they run.

options.text_md: It scripts: whatever you typed once, you can save and run again.
options.why_md: Also true, and useful for a log you read every week. It does not explain why the server offers only a prompt.

options.text_md: It works over `ssh`: every server you will ever touch has a terminal, and nothing else.
options.why_md: Right: slide 6 gives exactly this as one of its reasons. A server is managed from a command line because that is all it is guaranteed to have.

options.text_md: CI is a terminal: the check workflow is a list of commands another computer types.
options.why_md: True, and the same idea (the machine at the other end has no screen to click). But the situation here is a server reached by `ssh`, which slide 6 names separately.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 6 lists reasons why a 50-year-old interface survived: it composes, it scripts, it works over `ssh`, CI is a terminal, and "a GUI is for doing something once, a terminal for doing it a hundred times". They are all true; the question is which one fits the situation. A rented server, reached from your laptop, has to work with whatever every server has, which is a command line. That is the `ssh` reason, in the slide's words: "every server you will ever touch has one, and nothing else". Pipes and scripts then make that prompt worth having.
